content: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common form of muscular dystrophy in children. It is an incurable disease with X-linked recessive inheritance, characterized by progressive muscle wasting and loss of walking ability. Without treatment, most patients become completely dependent on a wheelchair by the age of 13. A primary goal of treatment is to prolong the ability to walk. Evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) has shown that corticosteroids significantly improve muscle strength and function in boys with DMD over the short term (six months) and improve muscle strength at two years, although data on functional outcomes at two years are limited. Corticosteroids are now a standard part of care for DMD, but questions remain regarding their long-term effects, the optimal timing to initiate treatment, the balance of benefits versus side effects over time, and the choice of corticosteroid or dosing regimen. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of corticosteroids on walking ability, muscle strength, functional capacity, and quality of life in DMD patients. It also aimed to determine whether the benefits of corticosteroids are sustained over the long term (beyond two years), assess adverse effects, and compare the efficacy and side effects of different corticosteroid preparations and dosing regimens. The review included 12 studies with a total of 667 participants, as well as two ongoing studies. Six RCTs were newly added in this update, and important non-randomized cohort studies were also considered. However, some significant studies remain unpublished, and not all published studies provided complete outcome data. One two-year RCT involving deflazacort (n = 28) used prolongation of walking ability as an outcome measure, but the data were insufficient to draw conclusions. Meta-analyses of secondary outcomes showed that corticosteroids, specifically prednisone or prednisolone at a dose of 0.75 mg/kg/day, improved muscle strength and function compared to placebo over six months. Moderate-quality evidence from up to four RCTs supported these findings. A single trial demonstrated that 0.75 mg/kg/day was superior to 0.3 mg/kg/day for most measures of strength and function, with little additional benefit observed at a dose of 1.5 mg/kg/day. Improvements were noted in measures such as Gowers' time (time taken to rise from the floor), timed walking tests, four-stair climbing time, ability to lift weights, leg function grade, and forced vital capacity. One new RCT (n = 66) reported better muscle strength, functional outcomes, and quality of life with daily prednisone at a dose of 0.75 mg/kg/day over 12 months. Another RCT (n = 28) showed that deflazacort stabilized muscle strength compared to placebo over two years, but the results of timed functional tests were too imprecise to draw firm conclusions. A double-blind RCT (n = 64) compared daily prednisone (0.75 mg/kg/day) with weekend-only prednisone (5 mg/kg/weekend day) and found no significant difference in muscle strength and function over 12 months. However, the quality of evidence was moderate to low. Two small RCTs (n = 52) compared daily prednisone (0.75 mg/kg/day) with daily deflazacort (0.9 mg/kg/day), but methodological limitations prevented a clear comparison of muscle strength or function between the two drugs. Adverse effects of corticosteroids were common and included excessive weight gain, behavioral abnormalities, cushingoid appearance, and excessive hair growth. Moderate-quality evidence indicated that behavioral changes and weight gain were more frequent with corticosteroids than with placebo. Hair growth and cushingoid features were more common at a dose of 0.75 mg/kg/day compared to 0.3 mg/kg/day of prednisone. When comparing daily prednisone with weekend-only prednisone, both groups experienced weight gain, but there was no clear difference in body mass index (BMI) or behavioral changes. However, the weekend-only group showed a greater increase in height. Very low-quality evidence suggested that deflazacort caused less weight gain than prednisone after 12 months of treatment, with no difference in behavioral abnormalities. Data were insufficient to assess the risk of fractures or cataracts for any comparison. Non-randomized studies supported the findings of RCTs, showing functional benefits from corticosteroids that were sustained for up to 66 months. However, adverse effects were common, though generally manageable. A large comparative longitudinal study of daily versus intermittent corticosteroid regimens (10 days on, 10 days off) over an average of four years suggested that a daily regimen prolonged walking ability and improved functional scores in children over the age of seven. However, the daily regimen was associated with a higher frequency of side effects compared to the intermittent regimen. In conclusion, moderate-quality evidence from RCTs indicates that corticosteroid therapy improves muscle strength and function in DMD over the short term (up to 12 months) and improves muscle strength up to two years. The evidence for the efficacy of a 0.75 mg/kg/day dose of prednisone or higher is relatively robust. However, there is no RCT evidence to confirm the effect of corticosteroids on prolonging walking ability. In the short term, adverse effects were more common with corticosteroids than with placebo, but they were not clinically severe. A weekend-only prednisone regimen appears to be as effective as daily prednisone over 12 months, with no clear difference in BMI. Very low-quality evidence suggests that deflazacort may cause less weight gain than prednisone after one year of treatment. Long-term benefits and risks of corticosteroid treatment, as well as intermittent regimens, cannot be adequately assessed from the available RCTs. Non-randomized studies support the functional benefits of corticosteroids but also highlight significant adverse effects with long-term use and potential differences in efficacy between daily and weekend-only regimens over the long term. These findings have important implications for future research and clinical practice.
